name: Daria Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run operations at Greywater, a farm owned by a community land trust, which means the land belongs to a charity and the local members, not to one family. It's 180 hectares with sheep, a few pigs, and four hectares of vegetables. We pack about 600 veg boxes a week for families around the town. My day is half in the field moving sheep fences and half on my laptop planning it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that it all connects: the sheep graze a field, the field grows better carrots the year after. I use AI every day, honestly, for grazing plans from satellite pictures and for sorting the box orders. What wears me out is the gap between what's possible and what our tiny budget allows. I'd love a weeding robot and we can't afford one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still worth using where it helps, and I'd post some of my grazing maps to show what a small farm can do with it. At the trust's members' meeting I'd say we keep using it for the boring bits. No drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit let down. I was hoping it would get good enough to make small farms like ours competitive with the big ones. In this picture we stay small and stretched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the tools I use, keep the job, keep saving. I'd probably start applying for a grant for a second-hand weeding robot anyway, since they exist already. And I'd teach Hamid, our new trainee, to use the grazing planner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little bored. It's the future where nothing exciting happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound almost disappointed.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I don't want people to lose jobs, I'm not like that. But the hype promised that small, careful farms could finally afford good tools. Without that, the big ones keep winning on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend your own time on, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep pushing the trust to share machines with the two other community farms nearby. One weeding robot between three farms, booked like a village hall. That's my dream, really.

S0.say: It's still worth using where it helps, so I'd post my grazing maps to show what a small farm can do. At the members' meeting I'd say we keep it for the boring bits.
S0.think: I'd be a bit let down, because I hoped AI would make small farms like ours competitive with the big ones. Here we stay small and stretched.
S0.do: Keeps her daily AI tools and her job, and keeps saving. Applies for a grant for a second-hand weeding robot, trains a new trainee on the grazing planner and pushes to share machines with two nearby community farms.
S0.quote: One weeding robot between three farms, booked like a village hall.
S0.fieldNote: Daria sees AI as a tool for small, careful farms against big ones, which makes the plateau a disappointment rather than a relief. She's clear she doesn't want job losses. Her ideas are shared and community-based, fitting her politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance for community farms, if we organise. I'd be in the farming group chats sharing what works. I'd also say loudly that big agribusiness shouldn't be the only ones getting cheap robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I come out of this well. I'm already the person who knows the tools, so I'd be more useful, not less. It feels a bit unfair to say that out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the weeding robot in the first year, through a grant or a loan from the trust. I'd do a short online course in farm data so I could fix things myself. And I'd write a plan for how the hours saved on weeding go into a second veg box round, so nobody loses work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited. Some guilt mixed in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Greywater would feel this the most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The seasonal weeders. We hire six people every summer to hand-weed the carrots. If a robot does that, those six don't come back. Some of them are students and won't mind, but two are local mums who rely on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the trust board gets scared and doesn't move. Then the big farms get cheaper and cheaper and we lose our box customers. So the worry is going too slow, not too fast.

S1.say: This is the chance for community farms if we organise, and big agribusiness shouldn't be the only ones getting cheap robots. I'd share what works in the farming group chats.
S1.think: I come out of this well, because I already know the tools and would be more useful, not less. It feels a bit unfair to say that out loud.
S1.do: Brings in a weeding robot in the first year through a grant or a trust loan and takes a short online course in farm data. Plans to move the saved weeding hours into a second veg box round so nobody loses work.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with some guilt.
S1.quote: So the worry is going too slow, not too fast.
S1.fieldNote: She expects to do well and feels guilty about it. She's specific about who loses: six summer weeders, two of whom are local mothers who rely on the work. Her fear runs opposite to most people's: that her board moves too slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs to be public, or it'll be a disaster. If robots can farm, the food system has to be owned by the people who eat from it, not a handful of tech companies. I'd be saying that everywhere, and I'd join whatever campaign was pushing for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not that scared for myself. I've got savings, I know the tools, and somebody has to run the robots for a while. I'm scared for the town. Half the people who buy our veg boxes would lose their jobs at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put most of my savings into a members' share in the trust so it can buy machines before the prices jump. I'd automate as much of Greywater as I could in year one, so we stay alive. And I'd go to every council meeting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for me, for everyone around me. It's a strange feeling, being okay in a mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What changes about your own plans in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means no time for anything slow. No degree, no new career. I'd put everything into making Greywater one of the farms that survives, because if it survives, it can feed people who've lost work. That's the plan, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be in charge of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ordinary people through governments and co-ops. Not the companies that make it, and not big landowners. I know that sounds naive. But food's too important to leave to whoever owns the robots.

S2.say: This needs to be public or it'll be a disaster. If robots can farm, the food system has to be owned by the people who eat from it, not a handful of tech companies.
S2.think: I'm not that scared for myself, because I've got savings and know the tools. I'm scared for the town, because half our veg box customers would lose their jobs at the same time.
S2.do: Puts most of her savings into a members' share in the trust so it can buy machines before prices jump. Automates as much of the farm as possible in year one and attends every council meeting on the issue.
S2.feel: Anxious for everyone around her while feeling personally safe, which she finds strange.
S2.quote: It's a strange feeling, being okay in a mess.
S2.fieldNote: Her anxiety is about her community, not her own income. She's willing to put her own savings at risk to keep the trust farm alive. Two years rules out anything slow, so she bets on one thing she knows well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to build a public system for this, and we'd better start on Monday. Community farms, public robot pools, retraining that's actually paid. I'd say it in the trust newsletter first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a sweet spot for someone like me. I'd have time to build something, not just react. I'd be 32 when it lands, which is about when I'd want to be doing something bigger anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a network of the three community farms near us, sharing robots and data. I'd look at a part-time master's in food systems, two evenings a week. I'd automate the vegetables in year one and the sheep handling later, once the kit is proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy. When I'm busy I don't worry as much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time let you do that the fast one didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plan instead of grab. In the fast one I'd be buying whatever I could get. Here I'd have time to get the trust, the council and the other farms to agree on something together, which takes ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said putting your savings in the trust. Would you still do that here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it. Maybe a third. I'd keep the rest, because with five years I can be a bit more careful. And I'd want to see how the network goes first.

S3.say: We have five years to build a public system for this, with community farms, public robot pools and properly paid retraining, so we'd better start on Monday.
S3.think: Five years is a sweet spot for me, with time to build something rather than react. I'd be 32 when it lands, which is when I'd want to do something bigger anyway.
S3.do: Sets up a network of three nearby community farms to share robots and data and considers a part-time master's in food systems. Automates the vegetables in year one and puts about a third of her savings into the trust.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, which keeps the worry down.
S3.quote: In the fast one I'd be buying whatever I could get.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time changes her from grabbing to planning. She's realistic that getting a council and three farms to agree is slow. She becomes a bit more careful with her money when the timeline stretches, which shows the earlier all-in move was driven by panic for the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get this right, so there's no excuse. I'd be pushing for a public plan for food and farming. I'd probably be quite boring about it at parties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it looks good for me. I'd have a decade of building on top of skills I already have. I'm 27 and I already use these tools daily, so I'd grow up with the change rather than get hit by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the five-year one, but slower and calmer. I'd take the master's, build the farm network, and maybe stand for the trust board in a couple of years. I'd keep most of my savings and invest in the network only when it's working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you to 37. How does that look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I'd want to be running the network, or something like it, across the region. I might have kids by then, I might not. I don't plan my life around that. I'd want them to grow up eating food grown by people they know, even if robots do the weeding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the slow version that bothers you more than the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, actually. With ten years, people relax. The board says, oh, there's plenty of time, and then it's year eight and nobody's done anything. The fast one at least forces people to move.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to get this right, so there's no excuse. I'd be pushing for a public plan for food and farming, and I'd be quite boring about it at parties.
S4.think: It looks good for me, a decade of building on skills I already have. I'm 27 and use these tools daily, so I'd grow up with the change rather than get hit by it.
S4.do: Takes a master's in food systems, builds the regional farm network and considers standing for the trust board. Keeps most of her savings and invests in the network only once it works.
S4.fieldNote: Her worry with a long timeline is that others will waste it, not that she'll be harmed. Life plans like children don't drive her decisions. She sees herself as someone who grows up with the change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because of the town, not me. Half our customers losing their jobs in the same year, and nothing set up to catch them. What would help is public money for community farms to buy robots together, and a guaranteed income for people while they find their feet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who's excited. Everyone assumes farmers dread this. Some of us have been waiting for tools that let a small farm stand up to a giant one. I'd grow up with the change rather than get hit by it, and I'd like more people my age to feel that way.

headlineQuote: Some of us have been waiting for tools that let a small farm stand up to a giant one.
portrait: Daria Ito is a 27-year-old operations lead at Greywater, a community land trust farm with sheep, pigs and a veg box scheme for 600 families. She uses AI every day for grazing plans and orders, and sees robots as a chance for small farms to compete with big agribusiness. She stays calm about her own future in every picture, but the fast AGI picture makes her anxious for the town and its workers. Her answers are about shared machines, public ownership of the food system and a regional network of community farms, and her biggest fear with a long timeline is that people will waste it.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because half the farm's customers could lose their jobs in the same year with nothing set up to catch them.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for community farms to buy robots together, and a guaranteed income for people while they find their feet.
